cli.usage:
usage: burnlens <index|report|diag|probe|cohort|show|serve|sources> [flags]

  index   [--force] [--source ID] [--root DIR] [--db PATH]
  report  [--days N] [--metric usd|weighted|raw] [--by project,agent,...] [--top N] [--source ID]
  diag    [--days N|all] [--metric usd|weighted|raw] [--top N] [--project P] [--agent A]
          cost of the assembled context, outliers vs own median, cost per unit
          of output, tails, and what happened to the runs
  probe   [ID] [--run [--force]] [--days N|all] [--top N] [--metric M]
          your own regex rules over the logs: no arguments — list the rules,
          --run runs them over the corpus, with an ID — a report for one rule
  cohort  [--session ID --agent NAME [--workflow ID]] [--scan N] [--top N]
          what a subagent fan-out collected separately; without --session it
          looks for the worst fan-outs itself
  show    <link> [--json] [--source ID]
          the finding a dashboard "share" click pointed at: bl://… or http://127.0.0.1:…/s/…
          without an argument, prints the list of link kinds
  serve   [--port N] [--no-index]
  sources                      Claude folders the spend is computed over

Sources are added and switched in the dashboard (the picker top right);
the list lives at ~/.claude/burnlens/sources.json, each with its own index.

sub.one: {value} in them · {n} run cost twice its own median
sub.other: {value} in them · {n} runs cost twice their own median

outliers.subEmpty: no run went twice above its own agent's median

note.intro: The baseline isn't a dollar threshold — it's the MEDIAN of the same agent's runs. An expensive planner and a cheap merger cost different amounts, and only the agent's own history knows which number is normal.
note.corpusBaseline: The median here is taken over the agent's ENTIRE history in the index, not this session: a session rarely gives one agent five runs, and judging by three means comparing a fan-out to itself. The "median of" column shows how many runs it rests on.
note.sessionBaseline: Runs from ×2 the median make the list; agents with fewer than five runs are never judged — they have no median yet.
note.tail: A row at ×3 or above is highlighted: that's no longer spread, it's a different scenario.
note.unjudged: Not judged: {agents} — they have no steady task; one run is a two-turn question, another is a whole refactor, and spread between them is normal. Their spend shows up in "cost per unit of output" and in the tails instead.

byAgent.title: Who has outliers regularly
byAgent.note: If a third or more of an agent's runs are outliers, that's not outliers — it's two different modes of work under one name, and the median stops describing anything.

unitCost.title: Cost per unit of output
unitCost.note: Two denominators, because agents hand back different things: some files, some one block of text. Both are shown — "per artifact" and "per 1k output". Expensive on both at once means one thing: the agent read a lot and said little. A dash in a column means the agent doesn't produce that kind of output (a reviewer doesn't write files) — not zero, and not a red flag.

calls.title: Most expensive calls
calls.note: A block's cost is the WRITE (putting the result into context once) plus the CARRY (the same block riding back to the server again on every following turn of the run). Carry is {carryShare} of the bill: {carryValue} of {totalValue}. So watch the "turn" column: a heavy Read on turn two of a forty-turn run gets paid for forty times; the same Read on the second-to-last turn, once.
calls.estimateNote: An estimate, not a counter: {calls} tool results are converted from characters to tokens by a fixed ratio. The order of magnitude and the row order matter here, not the third digit.

runTail.title: Run tail
runTail.note: The tail is the turns and money AFTER the last recorded artifact: recapping what's already saved, re-reading its own file, a final summary. The cutoff is drawn at the time of the last Write/Edit, so everything billed after it lands here. Runs that never wrote anything at all don't count: for a reviewer, router or matcher, returning one block of text IS the work, not a tail.

duplicates.title: One brief, many agents

note.one: The same dispatch text, sent out to N cold agents. Each recipient writes its own copy into its own cache, and each one is paid for: only the WRITE side is counted, {n} extra copy out of {dispatches} dispatches — {wasteValue}. Carry is untouched by this: it already belongs to whoever received the brief.
note.other: The same dispatch text, sent out to N cold agents. Each recipient writes its own copy into its own cache, and each one is paid for: only the WRITE side is counted, {n} extra copies out of {dispatches} dispatches — {wasteValue}. Carry is untouched by this: it already belongs to whoever received the brief.

duplicates.sizeNote: Size and overpay are an estimate from the argument's character count.

health.title: What happened to the runs
health.hint: events whose price is a consequence
health.note: No line item on the bill is labeled "compaction" or "retry". Here events are reconstructed from the log, and the money is attributed by what happened NEXT.

note.intro: The compaction call itself costs little. The event's price is the FIRST TURN AFTER it: the surviving context is rewritten into a cold cache in full, at the write rate. In any other report this looks like an ordinary expensive turn.

summary.one: {count} total across {n} session, {auto} on fill, {manual} manual; typical context at build time — {medianTokens}, total rebuild {rebuildValue}.
summary.other: {count} total across {n} sessions, {auto} on fill, {manual} manual; typical context at build time — {medianTokens}, total rebuild {rebuildValue}.

byDay.title: By day
byDay.hint: spend — for the whole day, not just the errors

note.intro: A 429 doesn't cost money directly — it costs TIME and points at the shape of the work. The "live runs" column is the answer: a burst counts as many distinct runs as were in flight when it hit the limit. A wide fan-out means that's exactly why it hit the limit.
note.summary: {bursts} over {days}; another {singles} single retries — not a fan-out, just an ordinary re-ask, and they aren't folded into bursts.

failures.title: Failed calls
failures.subtitle: {calls} of {allCalls} — {errorRate}
failures.note: A failed call is paid for like a successful one: the error text lands in context and carries on every following turn of the run, so an error early in a long run costs many times more than the same error near the end. Total {value} — estimated from character count.

scope.hint: these runs came from different workflows — only count together the ones that actually shared work:

summary.collected: {activeRuns} runs collected {collectedTokens} large blocks; {sharedTokens} of them ({shareOfCollected}%) were collected by more than one run. The cost of the repeat collection is {wastedValue} of the cohort's {actualValue} spend ({shareOfSpend}%).
summary.writeVsCarry: Of that, {wastedWrite} is writing copies into the cache, at a rate {breakEvenTurn}× higher than a read. That's removable with a shared prefix: neighbors of the same type already share the start of their request, and the second agent reads it from the first one's cache. Whatever it would have collected on its own it reads there too, instead of rewriting it. The remaining {wastedCarry} is carry: each agent resends its own copy on every turn, and inside its own context window it sits there independently of where it came from. Only fewer runs, a digest instead of sources, or fewer turns removes that.
summary.prefixNote: Moving it into the prefix isn't free itself: a block the agent would have read on turn {breakEvenTurn} rides from turn one in the prefix instead — the write is saved, the carry is added. Worth it as long as the agents would have reached it before {breakEvenTurnExact} turns (the write rate divided by the read rate); the "turn" column is the median across copies. With that caveat, moving it to the prefix returns {prefixRecoverable}. Tokens are estimated — {charsPerToken} characters per token.

miss.longInvalidated: cache reset outside the TTL — pause {duration} at a TTL of {ttl}
miss.hintExpired: The entry lived {ttl}; after a longer pause the whole context is rewritten from scratch at a rate {rate}× higher than a read.
miss.hintInvalidated: The pause was shorter than the TTL — the write hadn't expired. That means the head of the request changed (a tool schema loaded, the skill or agent list updated), and everything after it had to be rewritten. A longer TTL doesn't help here.

note.one: Only misses the hourly TTL would actually have prevented count as saved: a pause longer than five minutes but shorter than an hour. Misses with a pause over an hour would not have been saved ({lateMisses} of them), and another {n} miss happened with a live cache — the request prefix was reset there, and TTL length is irrelevant. Rows already on an hourly TTL (the main thread) are untouched by the recompute.

Misses with a pause over an hour would not have been saved ({lateMisses} of them), and another {n} misses happened with a live cache — the request prefix was reset there, and TTL length is irrelevant. Rows already on an hourly TTL (the main thread) are untouched by the recompute.

probe.intro: A probe is a regular expression that looks for a structured block in the logs and ties the hit to an agent RUN. A run has a price, so a hit can be priced in money — grep can't do that.
probe.scopeDesc: decides which text of the log even gets fed to the regex at all: a naive search
probe.scopeExample: over the whole corpus gives 4516 hits — almost all of them mentions of the contract in prompts and read .md files; over agent returns, 588. There's no way to filter that noise out afterward.
probe.emptyIfDesc: decides which capture counts as empty: of those 588 blocks, 535 are empty, but empty as the literal
probe.emptyIfExample: — that's a project convention, the engine can't know it. Without it the probe reports 588 incidents where there are 53.

action.deleteTitleBuiltin: A built-in probe can't be deleted — it can be disabled, and it comes back once the rule is fixed

flaggedPrice.noteFlagged: "Flagged" — runs where the probe found a NON-EMPTY block.
flaggedPrice.noteOthers: "Others" — runs of the same agent in the same window, with no non-empty hit.
flaggedPrice.noteBaseline: The baseline is deliberately its own, not a corpus average: otherwise the column would just measure that a planner costs more than a merger, which is already known. A ratio of ×1.5 or higher is highlighted — that's where the block stops being a log marker and starts costing money. A dash means the agent has no clean run at all to compare against.

groupBy.title: Breakdown by groupBy
groupBy.note: The breakdown key is capture group 1 of the groupBy regex. Rows with no key are excluded, so the column sum is less than the total.

pattern.label: Regex
pattern.hint: Group 1, if present, is the capture; otherwise the whole match becomes the capture. For a paired block, keep both the opening and closing marker in the pattern.

emptyIf.label: Empty capture (emptyIf)
emptyIf.hint: a regex over the trimmed capture: a match means the block exists but is "empty". This is your project's own literal, e.g. <empty>.

preview.noMatches: No matches at all. Usually the scope is at fault: try switching "Where to look" or simplifying the pattern to one marker and see if even that catches.
